## 2.1b

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)


liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))


autoplot(liquor, sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly US Liquor Sales",
    y = "$ Millions",
    x = "Year"
  ) 

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot: Monthly US Liquor Sales",
       y = "Log Sales ($ Millions)",
       x = "Month")

```

It appears that liquor sales increase in the summer (which makes sense) and then spikes during the holiday season. Overall, the seasons and variation of liquor sales grows over time which suggests that logs are needed.

## 2.2a

For ARIMA one lag of dependent, two lags of error, a seasonal difference with two seasonal lags and one error lag was chosen. For ETS it says forecast errors enter additively, that it has an additive undamped trend, and that the seasonal pattern is additive.

## 2.2b

We can reject the the ljung box test and say that the residuals are not white noise.

## 2.3a

There will be 216 forecast origins (336 months - 120 window = 216).

## 2.3b

The first forecast is Dec 2001 and last is Nov 2019 (it forecasts Dec 2019). Across the board, the ARIMA model forecasts more accurately in both RMSE and MAE.

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)
liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales), by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)


```

## 2.4

The horse race between ARIMA and ETS has DM stat of -2.8635 and a p-value of 0.004604 and hence we conclude that ARIMA is significantly better than ETS. Between ARIMA and SNAIVE the DM stat is -10.72 and p-value is 2.2e-16 and so we conclude that ARIMA wins this horse race as well.

## 3

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h=1)

liquor_combo_fc |> 
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))

```

Combo lands in between ETS and ARIMA, which makes sense since its just a combination of the two.

## 3b

```{r}

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

The errors are positively correlated meaning that there wont' be much gain in combining the models. They are estimating something similar and doing it in a similar way and with a DM showing ARIMA just does it better, combining them only adds noise.

## 4.2

```{r}
#| include: false
# --- data ---
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> slice(-(1:2))
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))
qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp = growth(GDPC1), cons = growth(PCECC96), inv = growth(GPDIC1),
            emp = growth(PAYEMS), infl = growth(GDPCTPI),
            unrate = difference(UNRATE), ffr = difference(FEDFUNDS),
            gs10 = difference(GS10)) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

N <- nrow(y); origins <- 120:(N - 1); actual <- y[121:N, ]

# --- fast: OLS VARs (a few seconds) ---
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1); M <- ncol(z)
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))
  x %*% B
}
fc_var1 <- NULL; fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

# --- slow: load saved BVAR results ---
fc_bvar_03  <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
```

```{r}
qd_raw <-  read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))



growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)


N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N -1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]


var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}


rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)

```

Across the board, the smaller model forecasts better. It does so across all variables besides gs10. The smaller model forecasts better potentially because it adding more variables just adds more noise to the estimate without any extra signal. I don't think RMSE would be fair since they were all on the same evaluation sample.

## 4.3b

```{r}
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The BVAR(4) with lambda=0.3 beats the OLS VAR(4) on every variable. The reason is that it shrinks the lags biasing the coefficients a little bit but in turn significantly decreases the variance. Compared to VAR(1), VAR(1) wins on some while loses on others which makes sense in part since both deal with decreasing the SE but one does it through shrinkage the other just cutting. At lambda=0.05 I think the model overshrinks and gets rid of information biasing the estimate more than it helps.

## 4.3c

```{r}
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

e_var4_ffr <- actual[, "ffr"] - fc_var4[, 7]
e_bvar_ffr <- actual[, "ffr"] - fc_bvar_03[, 7]
forecast::dm.test(e_var4_ffr, e_bvar_ffr, h = 1, power = 2)
```

Both DM stats are positive, so the BVAR(4) lambda = 0.3 is the better model . The FFR that has the largest RMSE is only barely significant suggesting that the small gaps in 4.3b shouldn't really be seen as meaningful.

## 5.2c

```{r}
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

According to the appendix names, the first factor is showing employment, industrial production, and manufacturing stuff and functionally is capturing real economic activity in the real economy. The plot shows how this responds to recessions (goes down). The second factor is loading on price indexes of goods and commodities and transportation so its capturing the inflation shocks.
